His kind of rapping, based in a tradition of boasts and put-downs that stretches back beyond the blues, was being superannuated by gangsta rap, politically conscious rap, basically any rap that wasn’t about the everlasting amazingness of LL Cool J. Still only 22, LL was looking old. Did the force field of ego flicker? It did not. It redoubled in strength. It swelled with a mighty vibration. I’m gonna take this itty-bitty world by storm / And I’m just getting warm . In this song, over a scorchingly treated loop from James Brown’s “Funky Drummer,” LL spews threats, lands punch lines, and shares visions, expanding to such clanking self-magnitude that the rest of rap music is temporarily blotted out. A hallucination of personal greatness, becoming—while the song lasts—a fact. A Boy Named Sue Johnny Cash To hear that grave voice humorously aroused, that rich, austere voice in a register of levity—it’s like someone has found a joke in the Book of Ecclesiastes. Johnny Cash apparently sprang this number on his band at the last minute, and you can hear them chugging along watchfully behind him, taking their cues from the lifts and the falls and the chuckles in his recitation. In this performance, three entities are creatively converging. First, the composer: that brilliant cosmopolitan Shel Silverstein, Playboy cartoonist, children’s author, hit songwriter, and—for the duration of “A Boy Named Sue”—cowboy poet, like Robert W. Service with a ’60s glint in his eye. Second, the singer: Cash, with his biblical marrow and his dark glow of charm, a ruefully commanding presence. Third, the audience: the incarcerated men of San Quentin, starved of entertainment, starved of love, aggressively ready to laugh, roar, feel. Johnny Cash liked playing prisons. He had a connection with men doing time: He knew it, and they knew it. He believed in redemption. (They might not have been so sure.) And this song that he sings them at San Quentin, semi-serious but very serious, is about fathers and sons, and fighting, and becoming a man in America. You can hear it: Inside the prison walls, every punch line, every witty Silverstein rhyme, lands like a revelation. Ghost Rider Suicide Suicide: You were either for them or against them. They were a Lower Manhattan art shock, a dividing line—Alan Vega’s phantom voice; Martin Rev’s distorted post-tuneful keyboard blast, like a melted robot trying to remember rockabilly music. Politically, they came out of anti–Vietnam War protests; culturally, they twitched and scurried in the fiscal necropolis that was early-’70s New York City. Bruce Springsteen was for them. Infatuated with the first Suicide album, he would soon be making Vega-like noises, those atavistic little hoots and yips, on Nebraska . But where Springsteen seemed to be testing the depth of his own isolation, Suicide was into the void itself, an infinite recession of burning skulls. “Ghost Rider”—inspired by the Marvel character, a motorcycle stuntman riding paths of hellfire—is the song of an American demon, nothing but glamour and nihilistic propulsion. Vega gibbers and swoons over a filthy, driving three-note electronic riff: America, America is killin’ its youth . What can you do but follow this trail of incineration across the sky? Mumblin’ Guitar Bo Diddley A mad professor disguised as a thick-bodied, black-hatted rhythm-and-blues man, Bo Diddley built his own guitars (they were square-shaped), and he built his own rhythms, which were the syncopated thunder of industrial U.S.A., the grating of machine parts, the thrust and clatter that would turn the blues into rock and roll. This song, seething with shakers and maracas, features his signature beat, the Bo Diddley beat— bomp, bomp, bomp, ba-bomp-BOMP —but sped up, with the swing crushed out of it, the better to display the wild moods of his guitar. Diddley was also a trailblazer in his use of the tremolo pedal, and you can hear that going on too: No longer an elegant after-flutter of sound, tremolo in his music was a crude force, driving, destabilizing, its signals overlapping, creating a rhythm and almost uncreating it in the same instant. American volatility, American innovation, American electrification. Guillotine Death Grips Has America gotten crazier in the 15 years since this leering, shuddering, articulated beast of a song was released? Or is it just that the craziness has broken the surface? In their desperate prime, Sacramento’s Death Grips seemed to have cornered the market on free-roaming insanity. Public-transport mutterings, cell-block din, oracular street rants, profane telepathic zaps, hissed rebuttals to the unheard voice: All were gleefully enfolded into their punky-clunky emergency hip-hop. For these guys, in Martin Amis’s phrase, every straw was the last straw. And they could make it catchy . Memphis Underground Herbie Mann Across layers of vanilla-smooth pop-jazz, the guitar of Sonny Sharrock comes creeping. Lithe, ductile, unsettling, glimmering with distortion. Something elemental is going on here, a confluence or collision of energies: The flute of bandleader Herbie Mann is charged with breath, whimsically fluttering human breath; Sharrock’s guitar is charged with hulking electricity. There’s something political too. Mann is white, heterodox but commercially oriented, a purveyor in this context of lightweight fluty whiteness; Sharrock is Black, a ferocious improviser and noisemaker—the fumes of the New York free-jazz scene are still on him—who liked, in his own words, to “shatter the tune.” And how they depend on each other, how beautifully it works, Mann’s little pointillistic puffs against Sharrock’s ragged current. When the guitarist opens up, everything around him—the tinkling vibraphone, the choogling drums—shifts, levitates, and begins to diffuse at its edges into a kind of blinding solar frazzle. The wildness is contained; the container is renewed. America, land of great imbalances—why can’t you do this more often? Institutionalized Suicidal Tendencies Hidden away inside ’80s L.A. hardcore punk, on a track so singular, it’s almost a novelty record, is one of the all-time great American monologues: ludicrous and desperate, solipsistic and righteous, a system-indicting suburban teenage mind-purge. Our narrator, Holden Caulfield with a skateboard, is having problems. He’s thinking about everything, and he’s thinking about nothing. His parents are worried, but they don’t understand. All he wants is a Pepsi, and his mom won’t give it to him. To look at, the members of Venice, California’s Suicidal Tendencies were not theater kids: They were gang-affiliated bruisers, and their shows were famously violent. But what a reading their front man, Mike Muir, gives here, hoarse with pain and thwarted entitlement. This is 1980s American suburbia: Adolescence is being pathologized, and the culture of therapy has a totalitarian shadow. They’re going to put him away. I’m Against It The Marx Brothers There’s a flavor of Lewis Carroll about Bert Kalmar’s lyrics here, a pipe-y whiff of old-school English nonsense: For months before my son was born / I used to yell from night ’til morn / “Whatever it is, I’m against it!” This, however, is American nonsense—bigger, shaggier, crazier. (And more Jewish.) Like its English cousin, it depends, for its proper discharge, on order. Authority figures, traditions, uniforms, syntax, meter: It needs the shibboleths of reason to present themselves for destruction. But only America, unchained immigrant America, could have produced Groucho Marx. Look at him in this scene, at the beginning of Horse Feathers . He is, for some reason, the president of Huxley College, solemnly robed, and the tassel on his mortarboard flips and twitches in a kind of organic irony as he addresses the college trustees. Then he’s away, singing his song of total opposition, American contrarianism raised to a pitch of absurdity, because Groucho would be against contrarianism itself. And it’s not satire either, as Lee Siegel explains in his seriously instructive Groucho Marx: The Comedy of Existence , because even the most violent satire implicitly takes a moral position: For Groucho, there is simply no satisfactory position at all. It’s Bartleby—“I would prefer not to”—on crystal meth. God Ray of Light Madonna It’s 1998, and Madonna’s club children are weary. The dance floor has drained and deranged them. They have reached the end of the night. So like a balm upon their parched receptors, direct from her all-mothering spirit, she flowingly bestows it: Ray of Light , and its beautiful title track. Mysticism, yoga, breath control. Healing beats. An infusion of wellness before anybody knows what “wellness” is. How many absolute bangers use imagery from the Kabbalah? Not many. How often can we connect a pop song with the Jewish mystical concept of the kav— God’s primal bolt of illumination into the darkness? And this song is a ray of light. The sweetly climbing guitar figure; the soul-elevating groove. Madonna’s voice—that tight, glassy, airless, unmistakable pop-ruling voice—is transformed. Now she roams, now she soars. The great American artist can do this, mass-market the revelation, make the mainstream gleam with the first radiance of the universe. Oh, What a World Kacey Musgraves Fall in love, and you fall in love with everything: Love for another will open your heart to the lovable otherness of the world. Is that the philosophical proposal of this song? I think it kind of is. Through wafts of pedal-steel guitar, she rises, the Texan country-pop queen Kacey Musgraves, floating with cartoon buoyancy past magic mushrooms and luminescent fish toward the you to whom the song is addressed. The obvious forebear here is “What a Wonderful World,” from 1967, Louis Armstrong’s rumbling beatification of everyday life. But the universe has deepened in weirdness since then. A more contemporary parallel might be Insane Clown Posse’s much-mocked but to me quite valuable “Miracles,” from 2009: Fucking rainbows, after it rains / There’s enough miracles here to blow your brains . “Oh, What a World” is much sleeker and lovelier than ICP, but it partakes of the same—what shall we call it?—experiential openness. Which is an American style of perception, an American freshness: everything shining, everything renewed. River Song Dennis Wilson What do you do if you’re a washed-up Beach Boy in 1977? If you’re Dennis, best-looking and most doomed of the Wilson brothers, you pull it all together—all the years of pain and knowledge and queasy close harmonies—and you make a solo record: Pacific Ocean Blue , of which this song is the opener. “River Song” is immense: a hair-raising, gospel-boosted thumper, proceeding at a gorgeous orchestral trudge, about the river that runs under us all, under all beauty and under all ugliness, bearing us along and carrying us away. Dennis the surfer, his voice roughened by time and substances, has drifted inland—into the veins of the country. (The song came to him in the High Sierras.) The city has used him up; the river beckons. Maybe it’ll do for him what it did for Huck Finn—cleanse the grease spots from his mind. Journey in Satchidananda Alice Coltrane When John Coltrane died, in 1967, his second wife and musical partner, Alice Coltrane, sought consolation in the presence of the guru Swami Satchidananda Saraswati, part of the second wave of Indian yogis to bring their teachings to the United States. “Anyone listening to this selection,” she wrote in the liner notes to Journey in Satchidananda , of which this song is the title track, “should try to envision himself floating on an ocean of Satchinandaji’s love.” It’s a busy place, the ocean of love: full of music. Spiny, ego-unwinding tamboura, keen as a sitar; Pharoah Sanders on saxophone, following the line of his breath; Coltrane’s harp. A classical pianist mentored into jazz by Bud Powell, in Paris, she had taken up this instrument only a few years before, and uses it here to put us all into a state of tingling harmonic awareness. Meditation and yoga have arrived in the culture. Listen closely, and you can hear America’s third eye as it flickers its lid, stutters, and then bangs wide open. I Got So High That I Saw Jesus Noah Cyrus Nothing is more American than a personal experience of Jesus Christ. And nothing is more American than getting high. So we need not look for irony here, or any level of sacrilegious naughtiness: Noah Cyrus—sister of Miley, daughter of Billy Ray—and her writing partner PJ Harding are offering this beautiful song to us with the glossy-eyed sincerity of the super-stoned, and the bony earnestness of the spiritually tweaked. Put away your metaphors. They really did get high, and they really did see Jesus, and this is really what he said. You just need me in your heart / Tennessee whiskey and love : Is this how Jesus talks? I’d like to think so. I’d like to think he has no scruples around derangement, chemical or otherwise—that he’ll show himself to the out-of-their-minds as readily as he’ll show himself to the sober. The music is devotional Americana, slo-mo but not sad, rootsy but with up-to-the-minute production. There’s so much Kingdom left to come : What a line. The Lion for Real Allen Ginsberg The spirit of William Blake visited Allen Ginsberg in 1948, in his cold-water flat in New York. Ginsberg heard Blake’s voice, and Blakean visions of eternity beamed themselves derangingly into his noggin. This is the American mid-century: into the great buildings of the metropolis, a shaft of eternity. Ginsberg’s world was rocked, and his poetic calling was crystallized. In 1958, he wrote up the experience in “The Lion for Real”—not an act of bombastic self-exposure like 1955’s “Howl,” the nervous-breakdown-in-verse that made him famous, but a bumptious, generous, wonderfully slapstick account of the losing of his American mind. This version, recorded more than 30 years after the poem’s composition, finds Ginsberg extra jolly, extra goofy, a kind of outpatient raconteur riding waves of broken jazz. William Blake has become the Lion, a complex golden presence that will neither eat the poet nor leave his front room. What does the Lion want? It wants what America wants: It wants you to face your own nature, your own mortality, your own disgrace, your own divinity. Waiting for the Sun The Doors Who says Jim Morrison wasn’t a great American poet? At first flash of Eden / We raced down to the sea / Standing there on freedom’s shore . What a vista: pristine, Emersonian, the dew-dazzle of original America. But this is 1970. The ’60s are over almost before they began, their great project incomplete. Consciousness remains unredeemed. And Morrison is a broken prophet: heavy, boozy, whiskery. He sounds bemused: This is the strangest life I’ve ever known . The following year, he’ll be dead. He can still sing, though—that croon of his, Bing Crosby with shamanic antlers. He can lift his voice in a wolfish shout too. The flower children have followed him into the darkness of Freud and Dionysus—weakened as he is, can he lead them now into the virgin dawn? It doesn’t look like it. The people are gathered on the beach, but the sun won’t rise, and the high priest sings his song over a long, withdrawing tide of American serotonin. No Sun to Burn (For Brass) Kali Malone Kali Malone is known for the drone. (I can’t help these rhymes.) And the drone goes on forever, but breath is finite. So listen carefully, after each long velvety curving-in-space note played by the ensemble in “No Sun to Burn,” for the discreet sound of a musician inhaling. An American composer based in Stockholm and Paris, Malone works with pipe organs, synthesizers, and—here—brass. “No Sun to Burn” is elegiac in its mood and countercultural in its slowness. The notes accrete, more of a formation than a sequence: It’s like watching a Civil War band being turned to stone while it plays “Woodman, Spare That Tree.” Can it cure your ADD? Your terminal fidgets? Probably not. But listening to it puts you into a different kind of American time. Whatever you’re doing, when this comes on, you’re going to have to stop: stop rushing, stop judging, stop arguing. Shake Appeal Iggy and the Stooges Wild American beauty: Iggy Pop in 1973. Big night-creature eyes and the body of an acrobat—like David, if Michelangelo had sculpted him with a welding torch. Like David if he came from a Michigan trailer park. Iggy’s career, however, was in the dumps. Even the tiny constituency of rock-and-roll recidivists that he’d earned as fans with the first couple of Stooges albums seemed to have lost interest. No one appreciated him. No one? Not quite no one. David Bowie, the parasite genius, the man with the waving antennae and the sci-fi taste buds, had battened on to Iggy. Wrangling him and his band into the studio in London, Bowie mixed Raw Power as a thin scream of sound, a narrow infernal transmission. “Shake Appeal” was Iggy’s favorite track: the closest he ever came, as he later expressed, to being Little Richard. It is indeed shudderingly pure and very danceable rock and roll: The Stooges guitarist James Williamson obliges with a primal solo, a sequence of shrieking but cleanly phrased Chuck Berry–isms. The incoming generation of upstarts would idolize Iggy as the Godfather of Punk, but here he’s nothing more or less than an electrically enhanced child of ’50s America: chest-baring, goofily intrepid, rock-and-roll-adoring, whooping it up, bouncing into the future with Looney Tunes resilience. Like a Ship (Without a Sail) Pastor T. L. Barrett and the Youth for Christ Choir The massed voices of the Youth for Christ Choir, from the South Side of Chicago, are at moments in this song almost too seraphically strident: They scrape at the underside of heaven. But what a contrast they offer, what a celestial counterpoint, to the worldly, funky, individual, all-too-human, and very much down-here-with-us voice of Pastor T. L. Barrett, to his ecstasy of personal fallibility. I search for pleasure / But I found pain . Are you listening, young people? This is America’s great and constant sermon: By all means, gratify yourself, but in the end, it won’t be enough. You’re going to need community, and—unspoken in this song, but present in the vertical noise of the choir—a dose of grace from above. items.title: A la découverte de l’Ekikoveko, plat traditionnel Hema, avec le Prof. Bagamba Arali.
items.description: Aujourd’hui, Identité Culturelle met à l’honneur un mets emblématique du peuple Hema : l’Ekikoveko. Préparé avec de la banane plantain et du beurre frais, ce plat chaud est traditionnellement servi au gendre lors du mariage coutumier. Mais au-delà de la recette, l’Ekikoveko porte en lui toute une mémoire : des valeurs, des symboles et un héritage transmis de génération en génération.

items.title: Thiamène Cayor : 346 patients pris en charge gratuitement lors d’une journée de consultations
items.description: Au total, 346 patients ont bénéficié, samedi 19 septembre 2026, de consultations médicales gratuites organisées à Thiamène Cayor, dans le département de Louga, par l’association « Thiamène Santé et Solidarité » (TSS), qui regroupe des étudiants en santé et en médecine originaires de la commune. Cette première édition, organisée en collaboration avec le poste de santé de Thiamène Cayor, a également été marquée par un don de médicaments destiné à faciliter l’accès aux traitements pour les populations bénéficiaires. Selon le bilan communiqué par les organisateurs, 185 patients ont été reçus en médecine générale, dont 90 ont bénéficié d’un déparasitage. La pédiatrie a enregistré 89 consultations, contre 61 en gériatrie et 11 en gynécologie, portant à 346 le nombre total de patients pris en charge. Les consultations ont notamment permis de relever plusieurs pathologies fréquemment rencontrées, parmi lesquelles l’hypertension artérielle, les affections gastriques, notamment le reflux gastro-œsophagien (Rgo), la lombosciatalgie et l’anémie. Les organisateurs ont expliqué que cette initiative vise à contribuer à l’amélioration de l’accès aux soins dans la commune de Thiamène Cayor, en particulier pour les populations qui rencontrent des difficultés à accéder aux services de santé. Ils annoncent, dans cette perspective, la multiplication de ce type d’actions dans les prochains mois afin de toucher les différentes localités de la commune et d’apporter un appui aux structures sanitaires locales. Des bénéficiaires ont salué cette initiative, estimant qu’elle intervient à une période particulièrement propice, avec l’hivernage, saison au cours de laquelle certaines pathologies peuvent connaître une recrudescence. Par Salla GUEYE

items.title: Palestinian gunman shoots dead Israeli in the West Bank, soldiers kill motorist
items.description: NEAR RAMALLAH, West Bank, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Violence flared in the occupied West Bank on Sunday when a suspected Palestinian gunman shot dead an Israeli man, police said, and Israeli soldiers killed a Palestinian motorist who the military said was attempting to run them over. The gunman opened fire from his vehicle at Israelis gathered at a spring near the settlement of Neve Tzuf, near Ramallah, according to the Israeli military and police.

items.title: Côte d’Ivoire: Elle perd le réseau et découvre que son compte Mobile Money a été vidé
items.description: Le Mobile Money a profondément changé notre façon de gérer notre argent. En quelques clics sur un smartphone, nous pouvons aujourd’hui envoyer, recevoir ou retirer de l’argent, sans avoir à faire de longues files d’attente. Mais cette simplicité a aussi son revers. Chaque jour, des personnes malveillantes exploitent nos petites négligences et certaines failles pour nous piéger et nous soutirer de l’argent. C’est précisément ce qui est arrivé à S.G.F. Une expérience qui montre qu’avec le Mobile Money, la moindre inattention peut parfois coûter cher. Suivons son histoire. S.G.F est une commerçante qui effectue quotidiennement ses transactions à l’aide de son téléphone. Un jour, elle constate soudainement une perte de réseau sur sa carte SIM. Ne pouvant plus accéder normalement à ses services Mobile Money, elle pense à un dysfonctionnement de son opérateur et se rend dans son agence afin de signaler le problème. Après vérification, l’agent procède au remplacement de sa carte SIM. Une fois le réseau rétabli, S.G.F se connecte à son compte Mobile Money. Mais, à sa grande stupéfaction, elle découvre que ses fonds ont été entièrement dérobés. Choquée par cette découverte, S.G.F décide alors de saisir la Police de Lutte contre la Cybercriminalité (PLCC). Les agents l’assistent dans les démarches de dépôt de plainte. Une information est aussitôt ouverte et les investigations permettent d’interpeller K.M.J. Au cours de son audition, K.M.J nie dans un premier temps les faits et tente d’en attribuer la responsabilité à son petit ami. Mais, confrontée aux éléments de preuve recueillis par les enquêteurs, elle finit par expliquer le mode opératoire utilisé. Selon ses déclarations, K.M.J repérait spécifiquement les vendeuses lors de leurs lives sur TikTok et récupérait les numéros de téléphone qu’elles communiquaient à leurs clients pour les commandes ou les paiements. Ces numéros étaient ensuite transmis à des complices travaillant dans des agences de téléphonie. Ces derniers procédaient alors à la désactivation des cartes SIM concernées, avant d’effectuer une nouvelle identification à l’aide d’une pièce d’identité transmise par K.M.J. Cette manœuvre leur permettait ensuite de prendre le contrôle des lignes et d’effectuer des retraits frauduleux sur les comptes Mobile Money des victimes. En plus de détourner les fonds disponibles sur les comptes de leurs victimes, K.M.J et ses complices prenaient également le contrôle de leurs comptes WhatsApp afin de se faire passer pour elles et de solliciter frauduleusement de l’argent auprès de leurs proches. Au cours de l’enquête, les investigations ont révélé que plusieurs plaintes avaient déjà été enregistrées pour des faits similaires, mettant en évidence la récurrence de ce mode opératoire. Pour conclure, K.M.J. a été conduite devant le Parquet du Pôle Pénal Économique et Financier pour répondre des faits de faux et usage de faux, de changement frauduleux de carte SIM, d’utilisation frauduleuse d’éléments d’identification de personne physique, ainsi que d’obtention frauduleuse d’avantage portant sur la somme de 5 134 600 francs CFA, conformément à la loi n° 2013-451 du 19 juin 2013 relative à la lutte contre la cybercriminalité. Les complices de K.M.J. sont activement recherchés. Leur interpellation fera l’objet d’une communication ultérieure. items.title: Sayon Camara dévoile « Wo Timbolo », une ode à l’amour
items.description: La chanteuse guinéenne Sayon Camara signe son retour avec une nouvelle production musicale. Intitulé « Wo Timbolo », ce titre se présente comme une véritable ode à l’amour, portée par la voix puissante et chargée d’émotion de l’artiste. Considérée comme l’une des voix emblématiques de la Guinée et de la musique mandingue, Sayon Camara puise son inspiration dans un riche héritage culturel. Son univers musical s’inscrit dans la grande tradition mandingue, tout en s’ouvrant à une sensibilité contemporaine qui lui permet de toucher un public au-delà des frontières guinéennes. Avec « Wo Timbolo », l’artiste poursuit ainsi son exploration d’un répertoire où se rencontrent tradition et modernité. La chanson est accompagnée d’un clip à l’esthétique épurée, qui met en lumière la beauté des paysages et des mosaïques culturelles de la Guinée. À travers cette nouvelle réalisation, Sayon Camara célèbre également son pays, dont les couleurs et les décors servent de toile de fond à cette déclaration musicale. Une manière de conjuguer amour, identité et patrimoine dans une même œuvre. Après plusieurs chansons ayant rencontré le succès, la chanteuse poursuit donc son chemin musical avec ce nouveau single, qui vient enrichir une discographie profondément marquée par l’histoire et les sonorités du Mandé. L’artiste est par ailleurs attendue à Dakar le 2 octobre prochain pour un méga-concert placé sous le signe de la fraternité entre les peuples guinéen et sénégalais. A.N

items.title: Soutenance de master : Adama Kafando explore la scénographie sous l’angle anthropologique du théâtre burkinabè
items.description: L’étudiant Adama Kafando a soutenu son mémoire de fin de cycle de master en arts du spectacle et des métiers de la création artistique (AMCA), option Arts de la scène, ce jeudi 17 septembre 2026 à l’université Joseph Ki-Zerbo. À l’issue de sa présentation, le jury a jugé le travail recevable et lui a décerné la mention « Très bien », avec la note de 17/20. Le jury était composé du Pr Bernard Kaboré, président, et du Dr Arouna Yaméogo, membre critique. Le directeur de mémoire, le Dr Pingdwindé Issiaka Tiendrébéogo, n’était pas présent à la soutenance, mais il a transmis une note de reconnaissance du travail de l’impétrant, qui a été lue par le Dr Arouna Yaméogo. Peu explorée dans les recherches consacrées au théâtre burkinabè, la scénographie est au cœur du mémoire de master II soutenu par Adama Kafando. Sous le thème « Approche anthropologique de la scénographie dans le théâtre burkinabè : étude de Bandiougou, mise en scène par Jacques Matthiessen, et de Pukri, mise en scène par Vincent Bazié, scénographe Issa Ouédraogo », Adama Kafando montre comment les objets, la lumière et l’organisation de l’espace scénique peuvent devenir des vecteurs de valeurs et de références culturelles. Adama Kafando a soutenu son mémoire de fin de cycle de master en arts du spectacle et des métiers de la création artistique (AMCA) À travers ce thème, M. Kafando cherche à comprendre la manière dont les références traditionnelles et les procédés contemporains se combinent dans la construction du spectacle. Pour lui, le choix de cet angle part d’un constat : la scénographie ne saurait être réduite à sa fonction esthétique. Il montre notamment que les objets, les costumes, la lumière et l’organisation de l’espace scénique participent à la construction du sens. Ces éléments sont également choisis en fonction du public, de la localité où le spectacle est présenté et des connaissances du scénographe. « Ce n’est pas uniquement pour rendre beau, ce n’est pas le décor seulement, mais ça fait passer des messages de valeurs culturelles », a expliqué l’impétrant. Deux spectacles, deux approches scénographiques L’étude met en parallèle Bandiougou et Pukri, deux créations qui ne s’adressent pas au même public et ne mobilisent pas les mêmes procédés scénographiques. Dans Pukri, destinée notamment à un public de spécialistes et de critiques, la lumière joue un rôle central dans la délimitation des espaces. Les objets traditionnels utilisés nécessitent, selon l’impétrant, une certaine connaissance du contexte culturel burkinabè pour en saisir pleinement la portée symbolique. À l’inverse, Bandiougou, conçue pour le jeune public, privilégie des éléments facilement identifiables. « Quand on voit un artificiel, quand on se reconnaît, quand on voit aussi la famille qui est assise au tout, on sait qu’on est dans une cour ; quand on voit les gardes avec la canne et tout ça, on sait que c’est dans une cour royale », a étayé Adama Kafando. La scénographie devient ainsi un langage permettant au spectateur de se reconnaître dans l’univers représenté et de comprendre plus aisément les messages portés par la pièce. Au terme de ses travaux, les difficultés rencontrées par l’impétrant, de ses dires, restent la mobilité du scénographe Issa Ouédraogo, dont les multiples déplacements ont allongé le temps consacré à l’étude, ainsi que les conditions de recherche à l’université. Mais malgré les difficultés, dit-il, « nous sommes parvenus au terme de notre travail ». Les membres du jury ont apprécié le travail de l'étudiant En effet, Adama Kafando estime avoir contribué à une meilleure compréhension des objets traditionnels mobilisés dans la scénographie burkinabè. Il a ainsi souhaité que son mémoire puisse servir de point de départ à d’autres recherches. « Je suis très content d’avoir, malgré certaines difficultés, réussi à soutenir mon thème. Cela va permettre aux nouveaux venus, à tous ceux qui voudront aborder un travail dans ce sens, de savoir qu’une personne a déjà travaillé sur la scénographie et que cela peut servir de documentation pour élargir dans d’autres aspects de la scénographie », a soutenu M. Kafando. Un travail considéré comme pionnier Dans son appréciation du mémoire, le directeur de mémoire, le Dr Pingdwindé Issiaka Tiendrébéogo, absent lors de la présentation, a transmis une note de reconnaissance du travail de l’impétrant, qui a été lue par le Dr Arouna Yaméogo. Dans cette note, le directeur de mémoire a donné un avis favorable à la soutenance, estimant que le travail répond globalement aux exigences d’un mémoire de master II en arts du spectacle et des métiers de la création artistique. Le Dr Tiendrébéogo a également estimé que l’impétrant a choisi « une question relativement peu explorée dans les recherches consacrées au théâtre burkinabè : la scénographie. Et ses recherches lui ont permis de dépasser une lecture centrée uniquement sur le texte dramatique, le metteur en scène ou le comédien », a-t-il dit. Pour le Dr Arouna Yaméogo, enseignant d’art pratique et de sémiologie à l’université Joseph Ki-Zerbo et membre critique, l’analyse relève également l’intérêt scientifique du sujet. « Peu d’étudiants s’aventurent sur la question de la scénographie. C’est une question délicate », a-t-il affirmé, en saluant le choix du candidat. Pour le Dr Kaboré, « la scénographie joue un grand rôle dans la consistance du théâtre ». Il considère, par ailleurs, le mémoire comme un travail pionnier qui mérite d’être davantage connu. Le membre critique a ainsi appelé à la poursuite de cette dynamique, notamment à travers la vulgarisation du travail. « Il faut qu’il serve d’exemple », a insisté le Dr Arouna Yaméogo, estimant que cette recherche peut encourager d’autres étudiants à investir des domaines encore peu explorés des études théâtrales. Nadège KINDA Minute.bf

items.title: Sid Ahmed Agoumi, monument du cinéma algérien, s’éteint à 86 ans
items.description: L’acteur et dramaturge Sid Ahmed Agoumi est décédé ce dimanche 20 septembre à 86 ans, a annoncé l’Office national des droits d'auteurs et droits voisins (ONDA). C’est un monument du cinéma algérien qui s’en va. De son vrai nom Sid Ahmed Meziane, le défunt est une figure emblématique du théâtre et du cinéma algériens. Sid Ahmed Agoumi, une carrière de plus de 60 ans Né en 1940 à Alger, Sid Ahmed Agoumi a un parcours artistique de plus de 60 ans, participant à des dizaines d'œuvres cinématographiques, télévisuelles et pièces de théâtre. Il a notamment joué dans « Z » de Costa-Gavras, l'unique œuvre algérienne oscarisée (1968), Les Hors-la-loi de Tewfik Farès (1969), Automne, octobre à Alger, de Mohamed Lakhdar Hamina (1993)… Installé en France depuis les années 1990, Agoumi a continué à apparaître dans des films de cinéma et de télévision. Il a aussi dirigé le Théâtre national algérien (TNA), les théâtres régionaux d’Annaba et de Constantine ainsi que la maison de la culture de Tizi-Ouzou. De nombreuses figures de l'art et de la culture ont tenu à lui rendre hommage dès l’annonce de son décès. Un homme « généreux, drôle, simple » L’ONDA a salué la mémoire d’une « figure emblématique du théâtre et du cinéma algériens ». « Avec son départ, la scène artistique algérienne perd une figure qui a laissé une empreinte indélébile dans le cœur de son public, ainsi qu’un parcours riche qui a fait de la scène et de l’écran des espaces de création et d’expression, et qui a contribué à enrichir le paysage culturel national par des rôles et des œuvres qui resteront gravés dans la mémoire de l’art algérien », a écrit le directeur de l'Office, Samir Thaalbi. « Sid Ahmed Agoumi nous quitte sur la pointe des pieds », a déploré pour sa part le réalisateur Bachir Derrais, qui dit avoir partagé avec le défunt « au moins un quart de siècle de travail, d’amitié, de complicité et surtout de fous rires ». « Une immense carrière, un parcours exemplaire, mais au-delà de l’acteur, je veux me souvenir de l’homme : généreux, drôle, simple », a ajouté le réalisateur à propos de celui qu'il a dirigé dans deux de ses films, Gourbi Palace (2006) et Llob (2009). « Adieu, Sid Ahmed Agoumi, artiste, homme et grand enfant innocent », a écrit de son côté le journaliste H’mida Ayachi sur sa page Facebook. items.title: AUC chief arrives in New York to advance Africa's priorities at UNGA
items.description: The Chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, arrived in New York on Saturday ahead of the General Debate of the High-Level Week of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA 81). Convened under the theme, "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All," this year's Assembly will provide a platform for the AU to amplify Africa’s voice and push for a more representative, equitable and effective multilateral system. Youssouf is expected to use the UNGA 81 platform to push various agenda for the continent. First, the AUC chief will amplify calls for Africa to have a stronger voice in shaping global decisions. He is thus expected to advocate for a more representative, equitable and effective multilateral system, including meaningful African representation in the UN Security Council and international financial institutions. Youssouf is also expected to assert Africa's stance that the continent is taking greater responsibility for shaping its own future. Here, he will highlight Africa's leadership and ownership around peace and security, continental integration and economic transformation, while advancing institutional reform and greater financial autonomy. He is also expected to affirm the continent's position that it is an indispensable partner in addressing global challenges. During his stay in New York, the AUC Chairperson is also scheduled to hold a series of high-level engagements, including a meeting with the United Nations Secretary-General, as well as meetings with various Heads of State and Government and leaders from the business community. The AU delegation will further use the High-Level Week to convene side-events that advance Africa's strategic priorities and strengthen partnerships towards a more representative, effective, and responsive multilateral system.

items.title: Tunis | Arrestation de l’agresseur des deux élèves à La Cagna
items.description: La brigade de la police judiciaire de Sidi El Bechir a rapidement appréhendé le principal suspect impliqué dans une agression à l’arme blanche contre deux élèves, aux abords d’un établissement scolaire du quartier de La Cagna, à la lisière sud de Tunis. L’agression a causé aux victimes des blessures de gravité variable au niveau de la poitrine et de l’épaule. Dès réception du signalement, la brigade a réussi à identifier, à traquer et interpeller l’agresseur présumé en un temps record. Le dossier a été transmis au ministère public près le Tribunal de première instance de Tunis 2, qui a ordonné le placement en garde à vue du suspect principal afin de poursuivre l’enquête et d’élucider le mobile et les circonstances de son crime. Par ailleurs, il a été décidé de déférer deux autres suspects devant la justice, afin qu’elle statue sur leur degré d’implication dans cette agression. I. B. items.title: Interdiction du voile : après Ségolène Royal, Dominique de Villepin prend position
items.description: Dominique de Villepin, potentiel candidat à la présidentielle française, a pris clairement position sur le projet de Marine Le Pen d’interdire le port du voile islamique en France si elle accède à l’Élysée en 2027. « Je ne vois pas l'intérêt de détruire la paix sociale dans notre pays », a dénoncé l’ancien premier ministre de Jacques Chirac sur LCI samedi, en réponse aux propos de Marine le Pen sur le port du voile dans l’espace public. « Manifestement Marine Le Pen n’a pas la moindre idée de comment redresser le pays. Elle veut ouvrir un certain nombre de boîtes, comme l’immigration, la réforme de la Constitution, de façon à jouer les Français les uns contre les autres en stigmatisant. Et pour quel objectif ? C’est parce que quand on ne peut pas répondre aux problèmes des Français, on exclut » , a-t-il dit. Marine Le Pen veut interdire le port du voile en France Mardi, Marine Le Pen a confirmé son engagement d’interdire le port du voile dans l’espace public en France si elle est élue présidente de la République en 2027. « L'objectif sera d'interdire le voile et nous le ferons si les Français nous en donnent mandat « , a-t-elle dit. Ce projet divise profondément la France. L’extrême droite et la droite sont favorables alors que la gauche est opposée. Avant Dominique de Villepin, qui a jugé dangereux le projet de Marine le Pen, Ségolène Royal, candidate à la primaire socialiste du 9 octobre pour la prochaine présidentielle, a tranché la question. « Je ne ferai pas la chasse au foulard », a-t-elle déclaré. « Ce n’est pas la chasse au foulard qui va faire baisser le prix de l’essence ou éradiquer la pédocriminalité », a estimé la finaliste de la présidentielle de 2007. L’article Interdiction du voile : après Ségolène Royal, Dominique de Villepin prend position est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Le Burkina et le Mali réaffirment leur solidarité à Niamey
items.description: Une délégation burkinabè et malienne, conduite par le général Célestin Simporé et comprenant notamment les ministres des Affaires étrangères des deux pays ainsi que le ministre malien de la Défense, a été reçue vendredi à Niamey par le président Abdourahamane Tiani, à la suite de la tentative de déstabilisation des 28 et 29 août. Le président Abdourahamane Tiani a reçu, vendredi 18 septembre 2026 au Palais de la Présidence à Niamey, une délégation du Burkina Faso et du Mali venue témoigner de la solidarité des deux pays après les événements survenus dans la nuit du 28 au 29 août, rapporte l’agence africaine de presse. La délégation était conduite par le général Célestin Simporé et comprenait notamment les ministres burkinabè et malien des Affaires étrangères, ainsi que le ministre malien de la Défense. « Au nom du peuple nigérien et en mon nom propre, je leur ai exprimé notre profonde gratitude. Cette visite est la preuve que l’AES est plus qu’une alliance, c’est une famille », a indiqué le général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani dans un message publié au terme de l’audience. « L’ennemi ne dort pas, mais nous non plus. Nous resterons debout et unis », a ajouté le chef de l’État . Prenant la parole au terme de l’audience, le général Célestin Simporé a indiqué que la délégation avait été mandatée par le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, président du Burkina Faso, chef de l’État et président en exercice de la Confédération de l’AES. « La mission consiste à apporter le soutien des peuples du Burkina, des peuples du Mali, des présidents du Burkina Faso et des présidents du Mali aux autorités politiques du Niger et à l’ensemble des peuples nigériens », a-t-il déclaré dans un message relayé par le ministère burkinabè de la Défense. Selon le général Simporé, cette démarche vise à exprimer « une solidarité sans faille » au Niger et à soutenir la poursuite de la construction de la Confédération de l’AES. « Ceci nous rappelle toujours que l’AES doit se consolider davantage, arriver à des résultats probants parce que l’ennemi, comme vous le savez, ne dort pas », a-t-il poursuivi. Le général burkinabè a également présenté les condoléances des deux pays pour les pertes enregistrées lors des événements. « La tentative a occasionné des morts parmi les loyalistes. Donc nous prions que Dieu les accueille dans son paradis éternel », a-t-il déclaré. Au lendemain des événements, la Confédération des États du Sahel avait déjà réaffirmé son soutien aux autorités nigériennes. Dans un communiqué parvenu à APA, l’AES avait qualifié les faits d’« entreprise de déstabilisation » et indiqué que la tentative avait été contenue par les forces restées loyales aux institutions. L’organisation avait également salué la loyauté et le courage des Forces de défense et de sécurité nigériennes. L’article Le Burkina et le Mali réaffirment leur solidarité à Niamey est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Sénégal : Sadio Mané lance un projet agro-industriel de 11,7 milliards de FCFA
items.description: Suivant les pas de son aîné Seydou Keita du Mali qui a fait des investissements énormes au Mali, le sénégalais sadio Mane vient d’investir environ 12 milliards de francs CFA au Sénégal. L’international sénégalais Sadio Mané a procédé samedi à Bambali, dans la région de Sédhiou (sud), à la pose de la première pierre du projet SM10 Agro, un parc agro-industriel dédié à la production, au traitement et à la transformation de la mangue, pour un investissement estimé à près de 11,7 milliards de francs CFA, rapporte l’agence africaine de presse. La cérémonie, organisée à Kountoubou, village natal du footballeur, s’est déroulée en présence du ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, Serigne Guèye Diop, ainsi que des autorités administratives et territoriales et des acteurs du secteur agricole. Porté par SM10 Agro, filiale de SM10 Sénégal, le projet prévoit une station de traitement d’une capacité de 8 500 tonnes de mangues par an, trois unités de transformation pour la production de pulpe, de mangue séchée et de beurre de mangue, ainsi qu’une plantation progressive de 500 hectares de manguiers Kent. Le complexe comprendra également un centre de formation, un centre de recherche et développement, un système d’irrigation et des équipements de mécanisation agricole. Selon les promoteurs, le projet vise à réduire les pertes post-récolte, renforcer la transformation locale et développer des débouchés sur les marchés sénégalais, africains, européens et moyen-orientaux. « Aujourd’hui, nous semons » Prenant la parole lors de la cérémonie, Sadio Mané a rappelé son attachement à Bambali et sa volonté de contribuer au développement économique de son territoire d’origine. « Aujourd’hui, nous ne récoltons encore rien. Aujourd’hui, nous semons », a-t-il déclaré, en soulignant l’importance de créer des opportunités pour les jeunes et les femmes. Le projet prévoit à terme plus de 1 000 emplois directs et entend favoriser la formation et l’insertion des populations locales dans les métiers agricoles et agro-industriels. « Une réalité tangible » Le ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, Serigne Guèye Diop, a salué une initiative qui, selon lui, illustre la nécessité d’ancrer le développement industriel dans les territoires. « Le développement industriel de notre pays ne doit plus être un concept abstrait. Il doit être une réalité tangible, ancrée dans nos territoires », a-t-il déclaré. Il a également insisté sur la nécessité de transformer davantage les productions agricoles au Sénégal afin d’accroître la valeur créée localement. Le ministre a qualifié le projet de « pacte patriotique » et réaffirmé l’engagement de l’État à accompagner les investissements productifs contribuant à la transformation industrielle du pays. Le démarrage de la campagne industrielle de SM10 Agro est prévu à partir de mars 2027, après la finalisation des démarches techniques et administratives. À travers ce projet, Sadio Mané entend ainsi contribuer à faire de Bambali un pôle de production et de transformation de la mangue, au service du développement économique de la Casamance. Vivement que cet exemple soit suivi par d’autres célébrités africaines. items.title: Libya asks ICC to support probe into attacks on civilian facilities
items.description: Libya has officially requested assistance from the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate attacks on critical civilian facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the western city of Zawiya, as stated by the Libyan Presidential Council late Saturday. This request aims to secure technical, legal, and judicial support for the ongoing investigations conducted by Libyan authorities. The goal is to share the investigative workload, establish the circumstances surrounding the incidents, and identify those responsible. Preliminary investigations by relevant Libyan institutions suggest that these attacks are part of a broader strategy targeting civilian infrastructure, including fuel storage facilities and power stations, thereby endangering the lives of civilians. The council reported that security agencies and the National Safety Authority have managed to contain some attacks and prevent others from occurring. Given the nature and seriousness of these incidents, they may constitute crimes against humanity or genocide, according to a legal assessment by Libyan authorities. Earlier this month, Libya's internationally recognized Government of National Unity announced the dismantling of an organized sabotage cell and the arrest of five Libyan and foreign individuals suspected of involvement in drone attacks on oil and electricity facilities in Tripoli and Zawiya. The government indicated that investigations are ongoing to identify additional individuals involved and the parties responsible for planning, financing, or supporting these operations.

items.title: Inondations à Coyah : La circulation est fortement perturbée ce dimanche
items.description: Au lendemain des fortes pluies qui ont touché la préfecture de Coyah dans la nuit du vendredi 18 au samedi 19 septembre 2026, la circulation reste fortement perturbée dans certains endroits. De la mosquée de Somayah jusqu’au pont de Sambaya, la situation est particulièrement difficile. L’ancien pont ayant cédé sous la pression des eaux, un important embouteillage s’est formé, rendant la circulation très difficile pour les usagers. Selon Aboubacar Camara, la circulation est devenue particulièrement dense depuis la rupture de l’ancien pont. Même constat pour Alseny Sylla, qui appelle à la mise en place de mesures d’urgence afin de rétablir rapidement la circulation. Au moment de notre départ des lieux, les usagers étaient toujours confrontés à d’importants embouteillages sur cet axe.

items.title: TTAP forms committee to consult with political parties, reach consensus on multi-party moot
items.description: Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) on Sunday formed a six-member committee to hold consultations with political parties and reach an agreement on the agenda for a proposed multi-party conference (MPC). The opposition had announced the proposed moot earlier this month. In a post on social media platform X, the opposition alliance announced the formation of the six-member committee, which will include: Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Allama Raja Nasir Abbas; PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan; TTAP’s Secretary General Asad Qaiser; Vice Chairman Mustafa Nawaz Khokhar; spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai; and PTI core committee member Khalid Yousaf Chaudhry. According to the statement, the committee will liaise with other political parties regarding the proposed moot, consult them on its agenda and work towards reaching agreement on the way forward. The notification said the committee would continue its consultation and coordination process under the guidance of the TTAP leadership. On Sept 11, the opposition announced it intended to hold consultations to call an MPC to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order and the economy. At the time, Barrister Gohar, speaking to the media after a meeting of his party with Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam–Fazl (JUI-F), had outlined plans to hold the conference, saying that “the current law and order situation, the economy, inflation, lawlessness, and the creation of new provinces issue” called for such measures.

items.title: Sudan: Six killed, dozens injured in Red Sea mine collapse
items.description: At least six artisanal miners have been killed and dozens injured after four mining shafts collapsed at the Oni El Dakkan mine in Jebeit Minerals locality in Sudan’s Red Sea state. Miners told Radio Dabanga that those injured were taken from the mine, near El Ansari market, to Port Sudan, about 300km away. An unknown number of miners remain trapped beneath the rubble, they said, as rescue teams continue digging to reach them. Mining sites in Red Sea state have experienced repeated collapses that have killed miners, amid what Radio Dabanga described as a complete absence of safety measures in mining operations. The latest report follows a collapse in which more than 80 miners were killed last week when mining shafts collapsed at El Zara mine near En Nahud locality, West Kordofan. Dozens more were injured in the incident. items.title: Macky Sall décroche au 3e vote de l’ONU et sort du groupe de tête
items.description: Macky Sall a quitté le groupe de tête de la course à la succession d’Antonio Guterres après le troisième scrutin indicatif du Conseil de sécurité de l’ONU. Le candidat soutenu par le président Bassirou Diomaye Faye a obtenu cinq voix favorables, neuf défavorables et une sans opinion. Le résultat marque un recul par rapport aux deux consultations précédentes, durant lesquelles l’ancien président sénégalais avait recueilli six voix favorables, sept défavorables et deux sans opinion. Macky Sall a reculé au troisième straw poll, alors que plusieurs concurrents ont progressé ou l’ont rejoint. Rebecca Grynspan arrive en tête avec neuf voix « encourage », cinq « décourage » et une « sans opinion ». La Guyanienne Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett suit avec huit voix favorables, six défavorables et une sans opinion. Le candidat sénégalais accuse ainsi un retard de quatre voix sur la première et de trois sur la deuxième. Les résultats publiés par senenews placent également Macky Sall au même niveau qu’Olara Otunnu et Rafael Grossi, qui ont chacun obtenu cinq voix favorables. L’Ougandais compte toutefois sept votes défavorables, tandis que l’Argentin en totalise huit. Avec neuf avis négatifs, le Sénégalais présente le bilan défavorable le plus élevé parmi les candidats ayant obtenu cinq voix d’encouragement. Le soutien de Dakar sans effet visible Cette baisse intervient après le soutien officiel apporté en juillet par le président Diomaye Faye à la candidature de son prédécesseur. Cet appui, intervenu plusieurs mois après le dépôt du dossier, n’a pas encore modifié les résultats enregistrés au Conseil de sécurité. La candidature de Macky Sall avait été transmise officiellement aux Nations unies le 2 mars 2026 par le Burundi, selon des documents de l’ONU. Le troisième vote ne traduit donc pas, à ce stade, de progression mesurable liée au soutien de Dakar. Une recommandation soumise à un seuil précis Le vote indicatif, aussi appelé « straw poll », sert à sonder les quinze membres du Conseil de sécurité. Chaque État attribue à chaque candidat l’une des mentions « encourage », « décourage » ou « sans opinion », mais cette consultation ne constitue ni une élection officielle ni une décision définitive. Pour être recommandé, un prétendant doit obtenir au moins neuf voix sur quinze et ne recevoir aucun veto d’un membre permanent. Le nom retenu sera ensuite transmis à l’Assemblée générale, qui compte 193 États membres. Les cinq membres permanents sont les États-Unis, la Chine, la Russie, la France et le Royaume-Uni. items.title: Colloque à Tunis | Les causes de l’infertilité et les moyens d’y remédier
items.description: Les difficultés à procréer sont un phénomène croissant au sein de la société tunisienne, a indiqué le président de la Société tunisienne de gynécologie-obstétrique (STGO) et chef du service de gynécologie-obstétrique de Bizerte, Mechaal Mourali, lors des travaux des 5 èmes Journées de la médecine reproductive, consacrées au traitement de l’infertilité et au recul de l’âge de la procréation, qui se tiennent les 19 et 20 septembre 2026 à Gammarth, au nord de Tunis, sous l’égide de la STGO. Dr Mourali attribue cette évolution à plusieurs facteurs, notamment la pollution et le mode de vie, ainsi que le stress, la sédentarité, l’obésité, le tabagisme et la consommation d’alcool et de drogues. Ces facteurs peuvent affecter la fertilité tant chez l’homme que chez la femme — en altérant la qualité des spermatozoïdes ou des ovocytes — et ainsi accroître les difficultés de procréation, a souligné le praticien, en expliquant que l’amélioration de la fertilité ne dépend pas uniquement des techniques médicales modernes, mais commence également par une modification du mode de vie — notamment la pratique d’une activité physique, la réduction du stress et l’arrêt du tabac — autant de facteurs susceptibles d’accroître les chances de conception. Les progrès des techniques de procréation assistée ont également contribué à améliorer les taux de réussite, a aussi indiqué Dr Mourali, tout en évoquant le rôle que peut jouer l’intelligence artificielle pour aider les médecins et les couples à choisir les meilleures options thérapeutiques, y compris pour l’évaluation et la sélection des spermatozoïdes et des ovocytes les plus appropriés. Le colloque a également abordé le rôle de la chirurgie dans le traitement de certaines causes de difficultés de procréation. Certaines interventions chirurgicales peuvent en effet contribuer à améliorer la fertilité et à traiter divers problèmes rencontrés par les femmes. Dr Mourali a insisté sur le fait que la combinaison de changements de mode de vie, de techniques modernes et, si nécessaire, de la chirurgie, offre de multiples options thérapeutiques pour faire face aux difficultés de procréation. I. B. L’article Colloque à Tunis | Les causes de l’infertilité et les moyens d’y remédier est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: The Pinball President
items.description: In 1946, the year that Donald Trump was born, the pinball machine offered everything but control. The bumpers were propulsive, the lights flashed, but the player’s only honest move was to pull a spring-loaded plunger. After that, the ball belonged to the machine, zinging and zooming wherever the bumpers sent it. This is how many Americans experience the Trump presidency today: antic caroming that they can do little more than watch. The ballroom. The Iran war. The threats against Canada. Greenland. Portraits of himself as Christ, a decorated general, or the pope. The arch. The Kennedy Center. Prosecution of enemies. Pardons. Imaginary Reflecting Pool vandals. Federal incursions into voting. Tariffs on. Tariffs off. Tariffs on again. The Qatari plane. Endless promises—to release tax returns, to end corruption, to deliver $5,000 checks—that never materialize. No president has been more with us than Trump, because no president has been better at seizing public attention. But there is a difference between getting attention and doing something with it. For months, the president has been unable to convince the public that he’s up to the job. In a CNN poll released at the end of July, 65 percent of respondents said that his policies had worsened the economy, and only 28 percent approved of his handling of Iran. Voters have watched the caroming and have concluded that he doesn’t have his eye on the ball. They care about the economy, and he seems to care about everything else. Only 27 percent of adults told CNN that Trump has the right priorities, down from 45 percent when the term began. And a record 73 percent said he hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important issues. In June, while Trump was fixated on the Reflecting Pool and stopping widespread voter fraud that doesn’t exist, a bipartisan housing bill aimed at high costs reached his desk. He called it “a big yawn” and said he hadn’t decided whether to sign it. In July, he let it become law without his signature. This is a problem for Republicans in November 2026, but it’s an opportunity for voters looking to November 2028. Once a roster of candidates emerges, their supporters will discover that the office demands—wouldn’t you know it?—exactly the qualities that their preferred candidate happens to possess. Now, when there’s no one horse to back, is the time to use the current president’s rat-a-tat treatment of our attention to ask how we want the next president to spend it. Many voters will ask only one thing of the next president: Don’t be Donald Trump . Fair enough. But stopping at “not Trump” wastes the extremity of the Trump years. Extremes clarify. A flood shows you where the ground was always low. The Trump years have been a reminder that the presidency is a trust. The public’s attention belongs to the public. A president borrows it, and the test at every turn is whether he spends it on their account or his own. Trump treats it as a possession, to do with as he pleases, like the East Wing. For him, the public is his cheering section. A president who ignores the half of the country that voted against him teaches them that elections are conquests. They will remember that when they win. [ Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer: ‘I run the country and the world’ ] It’s true that when Trump wants to focus the nation’s attention on something, he is relentless: immigration, his enemies, his ballroom. In April, The Washington Post found that he had publicly mentioned the ballroom on roughly a third of the days by that point in the year; he had posted about it more than about tariffs. But what he cares about often isn’t in the nation’s greater interest. A trustee doesn’t spend the trust on himself. The next president should ration his calls on the public’s attention, which, after all, protects his own effectiveness and the country’s. “Public psychology,” Franklin Roosevelt wrote in 1935 to a reporter urging him to speak out more often, “cannot, because of human weakness, be attuned for long periods of time to a constant repetition of the highest note in the scale.” When Roosevelt did speak, he explained. In his first fireside chat, he walked the country through how a bank works. Explanation is what lets a president speak less: A public that has been shown why can carry the argument on its own, and a public that has only been told what must be told again tomorrow. A president cannot push opinion where it doesn’t want to go, only nudge it, and that is possible only if he hasn’t already worn the audience out. A president who is always talking cannot use talking to signal that this time matters . The creed of this current era is the opposite. “If you’re not making news, you’re not governing,” wrote former Representative Matt Gaetz, who made news nearly every day he served and governed not at all. A president who consumes the country’s attention spends down a resource that citizens need for their own affairs, including those delightful corners of human experience that should be free of political consideration. The UFC fighter Bryce Mitchell understood this before the bouts on the White House lawn this summer. Mitchell, who did not participate, said that the government was “desecrating its role in society.” The government, he said, “is supposed to protect us, not entertain us.” Sometimes a president doesn’t have to ask for the country’s attention, because catastrophe has already gathered it. In these cases, a president can act as a moral force, particularly in consolation. Reagan after the Challenger explosion, Clinton after the Oklahoma City bombing, the younger Bush after the attacks of 9/11, and Obama at Emanuel AME in Charleston, South Carolina. Each president spent the nation’s attention on its grief and, in doing so, reminded the nation what it valued. Trump has nearly erased this part of the job, inventing a new one in its place: chief grave dancer. When Rob Reiner was murdered in December, Trump blamed Reiner himself; when Robert Mueller died in March, Trump wrote , “Good, I’m glad he’s dead.” A president sends a moral signal not just in the words he uses but also in what he chooses to spend them on. After the white-nationalist march and the death of Heather Heyer in Charlottesville, Virginia, in August 2017, Trump denounced the Nazis, but the thrust of his attention was aimed elsewhere. He obsessed over the counterprotesters. He praised himself for being the only one brave enough to name what he claimed were the misdeeds of the people opposing the Nazis. “You had a group on one side that was bad, and you had a group on the other side that was also very violent,” he insisted without evidence, “and nobody wants to say it, but I will say it right now.” He sent six tweets about Charlottesville and, in those tweets, never used the terms racism , bigotry , or white nationalism . He sent 37 tweets about NFL players kneeling during the anthem. All of this happens where we can see it. We tend to treat the presidency as if it existed only in that public form. Most of it doesn’t. Because much of the job happens in secret or out of camera range, what the president chooses to do with public attention is our best evidence of how he sorts the world in private. That evidence has limits. A president who never mentions the deficit might be working on it every morning. Eisenhower’s style was called the “hidden hand”: The president who looked idle at the podium was working the levers out of sight. But a president whose public attention shows no discipline, discernment, or patience isn’t going to discover those attributes at the necessary scale when the cameras turn away. Trump governs by the Heisman hand, always in your face. [ George T. Conway III: Unfit for office ] The presidency demands brutal prioritization. “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important,” goes a line that Eisenhower liked to quote . “The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” It was such a simple idea that it became the Eisenhower Matrix, used by managers everywhere to sort incoming challenges. The principle applies with more force in a job where the urgent arrives by the hour. If missile stockpiles are low, we want a president fixing that now, not giving a speech about the deficit. But we also want a president who can see the deficit coming and feel some obligation to the future citizens who will live under galactic debt. Trump spends a lot of his time on matters that are neither important nor urgent. The New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, who has covered Trump for 30 years, has said that if you charted his mind these days, 70 percent of it would go to gilding, construction, renaming, and tribute projects. The exhaustion after Trump will produce an appetite for quiet. It has happened before. George W. Bush campaigned on restoring dignity to the office because Americans were worn out by the dramas of the Clinton years; he wanted a presidency that his team promised would show up on page A24 of the newspaper. But quiet is not a standard. The office needs a benchmark built from the job itself, not from the last man to hold it. Nor should the next president react to Trump’s frivolity by turning every subject into a family talk in the living room about Important Matters—a brittle standard where partisans adopt the posture of the online scold who answers “I love dogs” with “Your silence on cats is deafening.” Under that standard, a president must speak to everything, and a president who speaks to everything has no time left to do anything. Campaigns often measure for qualities that have little or nothing to do with the office. But voters can evaluate how candidates treat public attention on the campaign trail and make some inferences about how they would approach the job. Here are some questions to ask: Does the candidate choose problems that a president can actually move, and can he say why those and not others? Can a president articulate a vision for the country to people who are not likely to vote for her? Can he explain rather than merely assert? Does she ever talk about a problem that won’t pay off before the next election? Can he let a news cycle pass without joining it? And when grief or outrage arrives, does he show any evidence of a concern for the entire nation? How a candidate handles these moments during a campaign—when public attention, ever more scarce in the age of the algorithm, is the only thing he has to spend—tells us how that candidate will spend ours. In 1947, the year after Trump’s birth, pinball changed. The flipper was added, which meant the player was no longer merely watching. Where the ball went was now, at least in part, up to the player. In 2028, voters will be in the game again. But that requires attention to the office now.

items.title: A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Emma Williams, an associate editor who helps oversee the magazine’s social media and has also written about her home state of Texas . Emma is a habitual rewatcher of Normal People , a show that she says has resonated with her differently over time. She also enjoys listening to her namesake Emmylou Harris, laughing over Adults episodes, and watching Hailee Catalano’s comforting cooking videos. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The television show I’m most enjoying right now: The first scene of FX’s Adults tells you pretty much everything you need to know about the show: It’s crass, crude, absurd, and indulgently hilarious . Adults pokes fun at Gen Z without being judgmental or predictable, and it features some familiarly ridiculous plights. Maybe don’t watch it with your grandmother—but your spunky aunt is probably okay. A quiet song that I love: I discovered the British DJ Fred Again when I was going down an NPR Tiny Desk Concert rabbit hole years ago. I was immediately struck by his talent—but over time, I have come to better appreciate the emotion he evokes through his performances. Even in his natural habitat, behind the DJ booth, Fred isn’t what you might normally expect from an EDM artist: He samples spoken-word poems, Zoom calls, and random internet videos to create songs that you can just as easily dance to as you can cry to. I know I’m cheating a bit by saying that his entire Tiny Desk production is my favorite quiet song, but the fact that he was able to pull off an acoustic EDM performance is remarkable. To re-create the sound of electronic beats, he used the marimba, the vibraphone, and the piano; he also pounded and tapped on a desk and layered in his soft, husky voice. It is gentle, engrossing, and stupidly impressive. A loud song that I love: The first time I heard “Dance Yrself Clean,” by LCD Soundsystem, I was confused. My best friend played it for me, and by minute two, I was enjoying the song, but I could not comprehend how this hazy and somewhat repetitive tune could continue for another seven minutes and be as “life changing” as she had promised. Then I hit 3:05 on the track. I felt the ba-da-da-dum in my bones before James Murphy’s newly impassioned voice flooded through the speakers. This is now my song for any moment when I need to drown out my thoughts. Whether I’m going through a breakup, a bad day, or an existential crisis, I’ll put on “Dance Yrself Clean” and itch through the first three minutes, eagerly anticipating the rush of euphoria that hits after the beat drops. Years later, that same friend and I heard the song live. I have no idea whether we were crying or laughing or shouting, but I know we were dancing with abandon—and letting the music wash over us. A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I watched Normal People for the first time when I was 19, and I’ve rewatched it at least once a year every year since. I have never wavered in my fondness for it, but my reaction to the characters and storylines has evolved with time. When I first saw the show, based on Sally Rooney’s novel of the same name, I fell madly in love with Connell, barely registering that his cold avoidance of Marianne in public was wrong. I just thought he was broody and complicated; therefore, to my teenage mind, he was perfect and dreamy. I’m glad to say that I have moved past that (kind of), and I now find it difficult to watch his treatment of Marianne in the first few episodes. In my 20s, I resonate more with Marianne’s college arc. Specifically, her need to become the coolest, most stylish, most successful version of herself—even if it comes at the cost of her own happiness. Marianne and Connell’s lack of clear communication is always maddening. But I understand it more with age. Sometimes vocalizing what you really want can be more terrifying than staying quiet. A musical artist who means a lot to me: I have to pay homage to my namesake, the inimitable country folk artist Emmylou Harris. Her music reminds me of my home state of Texas. Listening to her song “Boulder to Birmingham” transports me back to long drives through the plains of West Texas and the seemingly endless miles of wind turbines. I hear my parents’ voices, lovingly calling me Emmylou and Emmy-lou-lou. Whenever I feel adrift, her music pulls me back to the ground. A YouTuber, TikToker, Twitch streamer, or other online creator I’m a fan of: I have an embarrassing confession: There is a cooking influencer whom I’m really obsessed with—as in, I went to a meet and greet of hers, and I send her the occasional tipsy Instagram DM. (Sometimes she even responds!) Hailee Catalano is a James Beard–winning chef. Her food is fresh and unique, and her video style isn’t gimmicky or aggressive like that of so many other cooking accounts—it’s simple and personable. My favorite series of hers is called Friday Night Dinner , which is a collaboration with her partner, Chuck Cruz, who is also a chef and content creator. They film themselves making a new meal every week, and I can only describe their vibe as homey. The videos sometimes have awkward pauses and funny asides (and, of course, clips of their dog, Gus), and watching them makes me feel like I’m sitting at the kitchen counter as two of my friends prepare something delicious for us to eat. A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: The older I get, the more I find myself recalling the lines of Langston Hughes’s poem “ Harlem .” Hughes asks: “What happens to a dream deferred?” I recently turned 25, and the “quarter-life crisis” is certainly hitting me. I think about all of my childhood hopes that have dissipated, and all of the ones I still have that I’m not sure will come true. I, too, wonder what happens to these dreams. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : George Packer on sons and mothers Anne Applebaum: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption. What comes after America The Week Ahead Primetime , a crime thriller about the rise of the To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen and the world of televised vigilantism (in theaters Friday) Youth , a comedic-drama series about a 50-year-old divorcée balancing dating with caring for her aging parents and adult son (streaming today on HBO Max) Mazywood , a horror novel by Tananarive Due about a man uncovering the truth about his grandmother, set in Old Hollywood and the present day (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Alisa Gao / The Atlantic Math Can’t Go On Like This By Kai Williams In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.” Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all. Read the full article. More in Culture An ingredient that’s all too rare in adult life A shouting match and an ultimatum at the Kennedy Center The next change Trump has planned for the Smithsonian A night for actor’s actors, not movie stars The knives are out for Bill Belichick. Catch Up on The Atlantic What Trump’s bizarre posts are teaching us about AI Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is enormous. Ian Bogost: College is coming apart. Photo Album Willem de Kooning, Excavation , 1950. (The Willem de Kooning Foundation / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York. Photo by Robert Lifson.) Willem de Kooning took the language of drawing, ripped it up, and rearranged it, Sebastian Smee writes. Take a look at some of his drawings from a new exhibition about the influential abstract expressionist—and read about what he had to unlearn. Rafaela Jinich contributed to this newsletter. Play our daily crossword. Explore all of our newsletters. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
items.description: J ust over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions. Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform. In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.” Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree. Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality. Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example. [ Read: How to defeat a mafia state ] In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend. I n Guatemala City , I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt. For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated. That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him.
